summary: Give the Speeds and feeds calculator the min surface speed, the min rotation speed, the avg rotation speed and number of teeth and it returns tool/workpiece diameter. sections.title: How does the Speeds and feeds calculator work?
sections.html:
The Speeds and feeds calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports tool/workpiece diameter in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the calculator mode, the machine tool operation and the tool material); then you type in the min surface speed, the min rotation speed (Speeds), the avg rotation speed (Speeds) and number of teeth.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Speeds and feeds calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Tool/workpiece diameter=min surface speed ÷ (PI × min rotation speed)
Max rotation speed=max surface speed ÷ (PI × tool ÷ workpiece diameter)
Max surface speed=2 × PI × avg rotation speed × tool ÷ workpiece diameter − min surface speed
Min feed rate=(custom rotation speed × min tool chip load × (number of teeth))
Max feed rate=(custom rotation speed × max tool chip load × (number of teeth))
Min rotation speed=(machine tool operation, tool material, workpiece material, tool ÷ workpiece diameter)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Calculator mode set to Preset mode, Machine tool operation set to Drilling, Tool material set to High-speed steel (HSS) and Workpiece material set to Aluminum. Working through the relationship above gives Min feed rate = 108 mm/min, Avg feed rate = 108 mm/min and Max feed rate = 108 mm/min.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Min feed rate = 108 mm/min, Avg feed rate = 108 mm/min and Max feed rate = 108 mm/min should be roughly the size you expected from Calculator mode set to Preset mode and Machine tool operation set to Drilling.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Speeds and feeds calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the min surface speed, the min rotation speed and the avg rotation speed — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Speeds and feeds calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns tool/workpiece diameter, derived from the min surface speed, the min rotation speed and the avg rotation speed. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Speeds and feeds calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the min surface speed, the min rotation speed, the avg rotation speed and number of teeth, which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter tool/workpiece diameter in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Tool/workpiece diameter opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Min feed rate = 108 mm/min. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Speeds and feeds calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
